issues.legal_issue: Inclusion of legislation in the constitutional protection schedule prevents it from being invalidated for inconsistency with fundamental rights, with the protection operating from the legislation’s enactment.
material_facts: The estate-rights abolition regulation was challenged as violating the estate holder’s property right under Article 19(1)(f).
While the appeal was pending, the regulation was added to the Ninth Schedule.
issues.conclusion: The regulation was protected from the fundamental-rights challenge and was constitutionally valid; the protection operated retrospectively from the date of its enactment.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that legislation included in the Ninth Schedule is not void, or ever deemed void, on the ground that it is inconsistent with or takes away or abridges rights conferred by Part III. The Court held that this cures any such defect retrospectively from enactment, relying on Jagannath v. Authorised Officer, Land Reforms, [1972] 1 SCR 1056 at 1070.

predicates.challenge_to_legislation: A party brought a proceeding challenging the constitutional validity of legislation.
predicates.alleged_fundamental_rights_violation: The challenger alleged that the legislation infringed a fundamental right.
predicates.legislation_added_to_constitutional_prot: The legislation was added to the constitutional list that protects included laws from fundamental-rights challenges.

issues.definition: When legislation challenged for infringing a fundamental right is added to the constitutional protection list, it is valid against that challenge.

issues.legal_issue: A related notification that restores an affected holder’s prior rights and does not independently prejudice those rights cannot be invalidated once the associated estate-rights abolition regulation is constitutionally valid.
material_facts: The notification applied a tenancy-law amendment to the estates and restored the relationship between the estate holder and tenants that had existed before the tenants became deemed purchasers.
The Court held that the notification, considered by itself, restored the holder’s original rights and was not to his detriment.
The associated estate-rights abolition regulation was protected from the fundamental-rights challenge by its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the notification was rejected, and the notification was declared constitutionally valid together with the regulation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reasoned that, once the associated regulation was free from constitutional defect, the notification could not be successfully challenged standing alone because it restored the holder’s original rights rather than taking them away. The Court referred to the Governor’s notification-making power under paragraph 5(1) of the Fifth Schedule and to the regulation-making power under paragraph 5(2); the regulation’s protection followed from Article 31B and its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule.

predicates.challenge_to_related_notification: A party brought a proceeding challenging the validity of a notification connected with an estate-rights abolition measure.
predicates.associated_regulation_constitutionally_v: The regulation associated with the notification was held constitutionally valid.
predicates.notification_restores_prior_rights: The notification restored the affected holder’s rights to the position that existed before the relevant change in the parties’ relationship.
predicates.notification_independently_causes_no_pre: Considered by itself, the notification did not take away or impair the affected holder’s rights.

issues.definition: A challenged related notification is valid when its associated regulation is valid and the notification restores prior rights without independently prejudicing the affected holder.
